name: Schiedam
title: Schiedam Ship Repair UTM | Drydock and Afloat Hull Gauging
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement in Schiedam for ships in dock or at repair berths: renewal survey gauging, steel renewal marking, offshore and dredger hulls.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement for Ships Repairing at Schiedam
intro: Schiedam's waterfront on the Nieuwe Maas has repaired ships for generations, and the former Wilton-Fijenoord yard there now operates as Damen Shiprepair Rotterdam, with covered and open drydocks, floating docks and repair berths. Offshore and wind-farm vessels, dredgers, yachts and merchant ships come here to dock, convert or refit. That gives gauging what it needs: dry hulls, staging and gas-free tanks. For each Schiedam docking the technicians come from India, joining the ship on the yard's schedule.

highlights.p: One of the Schiedam drydocks is roofed, so hull work continues through rain and wind. For ultrasonic readings on bare steel, dry surfaces and steady lighting make the work quicker and the results cleaner, which counts when the docking schedule is tight.

highlights.h: Marking steel as readings come in
highlights.p: During a docking the yard's steel planners want answers every day. Plates beyond the allowable diminution are marked on the structure and listed by frame and strake as the work progresses, so cropping and renewal can begin long before the final report is issued.

highlights.h: Crane and pedestal work on offshore ships
highlights.p: Offshore construction and heavy-lift vessels come to the Schiedam riverside for crane installations and overhauls. Crane pedestals, foundations and the structure supporting them can be gauged and tested for cracks while the crane is removed or before a new one is set down.

port.h: Schiedam: a repair waterfront on the Nieuwe Maas
p: Schiedam lies on the north bank of the Nieuwe Maas, immediately west of Rotterdam and east of Vlaardingen, within the area managed by the Port of Rotterdam Authority. Seagoing ships reach it from the North Sea through the Maasmond and up the Nieuwe Waterweg, a passage with no locks, made under pilotage and with tugs for the final approach to the yard. The river here is tidal, with a modest range, and docking and undocking are timed to the tide and the current. Unlike the oil and container districts downriver, Schiedam's waterfront is not about cargo. Its value to shipping lies in repair, conversion and heavy engineering, and a ship comes to Schiedam because it is coming out of service for a while.

The yard that dominates the waterfront traces its history to Wilton-Fijenoord, a name that stood for Dutch shipbuilding and ship repair through much of the twentieth century. Today it operates as Damen Shiprepair Rotterdam and also houses the headquarters of Damen's ship repair group, an anchor and chain factory and Damen Shiprepair Van Brink. Its work covers refit, conversion, decommissioning, repair, maintenance and voyage repair, with particular strengths in offshore wind, dredging and yachting. Merchant ships come too, sent by owners who compare repair yards across North West Europe before fixing a docking. Nearby, crane and offshore equipment manufacturing gives the riverside another reason for specialist vessels to come alongside for a spell. The mix changes from month to month, but the common thread is vessels taken out of service.

A ship docking at Schiedam is in one of three positions: in a dry dock with the hull exposed, lifted on one of the floating docks, or alongside a repair berth for afloat work. Each changes what gauging can reach. In the dry docks and floating docks the whole bottom, the sea chests and the rudder area are exposed, and tanks can be opened in sequence. Alongside, the internal structure, decks, piping and tanks are within reach, while the bottom shell has to be gauged from inside. Offshore and leisure fleets tend to plan their dockings for the winter months between working seasons, so those slots fill early and the team's visas and travel are best arranged as soon as the yard confirms the dates.

facilities.h: Docks, floating docks and repair berths at the Schiedam yard
p: The Schiedam yard combines dry docks, one of them covered, with two floating docks and a row of repair berths along the river. In dock, the gauging team works from the yard's staging and access platforms, follows the class TM plan where a survey is due, and keeps pace with the surveyor's close-up programme. Lighting and ventilation of tanks are provided by the yard under the superintendent's contract, and enclosed-space entry follows the yard's permit system as well as the ship's own. Readings are logged as they are taken and shared daily, because at a repair yard a reading that arrives late can hold up the steel crew for a day.

The team is engaged by the ship's owner or manager and enters the yard on the yard's own induction and site rules. Before arrival the superintendent receives a plan setting out which spaces will be gauged in which order, matched to the yard's sequence for cleaning, blasting and staging. During afloat periods at the repair berths, the programme concentrates on what can be reached safely: piping systems, decks, internal structure and tanks that the ship can empty and ventilate. Owners whose ships trade regularly to Rotterdam sometimes book a Schiedam berth for a few days of afloat repair, and those days suit a focused gauging scope on a known problem.
list: Covered drydock — bottom shell, sea chest and tank gauging sheltered from the weather, useful when bare-steel readings need dry surfaces.
Open drydocks — full renewal and docking survey programmes on larger merchant and offshore vessels, worked from yard staging.
Floating docks — bottom and side shell readings on smaller ships, dredgers and workboats lifted for maintenance.
Repair berths on the Nieuwe Maas — afloat gauging of piping, decks, internal structure and tanks during voyage repairs.
Riverside quays where offshore vessels lie for crane and equipment work — pedestal, foundation and deck-structure gauging with magnetic particle testing.

context.h: Class surveys, port state control and refit decisions at Schiedam
p: A ship in a Schiedam dock is usually there because a survey is due or because the owner is changing what the ship does. In both cases the classification society's surveyor sets the extent of close-up survey and thickness measurement required, and the owner's superintendent decides how much more to gauge for their own planning. Conversions add another layer: a vessel converted for offshore wind work, a dredger lengthened or a ship being prepared for decommissioning needs its structure assessed against new loads or new rules, and thickness data is the starting point for the naval architect's calculations.

Paris MoU port state control applies to merchant ships throughout the Rotterdam area, Schiedam included, and a deficiency that must be rectified before departure can bring a ship to a Schiedam repair berth at short notice. EU rules shape the work as well. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation requires an Inventory of Hazardous Materials for ships calling at EU ports, and a refit or conversion is the moment when that inventory has to be updated. Owners facing EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime obligations increasingly combine structural repairs with efficiency work in a single docking, which makes the steel survey one part of a larger plan for the ship.

jobs.p: At Schiedam, the docking defines the job. The superintendent sends the TM plan, the survey status and the yard's work list, and we propose a sequence that keeps pace with the yard rather than holding it up: bottom and sea chests first while the hull is dry and accessible, tanks as the yard releases them, decks and piping alongside. Plates and pipe sections beyond the allowable margin are marked as found, so the yard's steel crew can follow the gauging team through the ship. Afloat repair jobs are shorter and narrower, and are usually built around one or two defects already known. Typical work includes:
list: A wind-farm installation or service vessel docking between seasons: bottom shell, crane pedestal and deck structure gauging, with magnetic particle testing at pedestal welds.
A hopper or cutter dredger on a floating dock: bottom plating and the hull structure around the dredging gear gauged, with wear readings on the pipework.
A product tanker in for its renewal survey: deck, bottom and cargo-tank structure gauged to the TM plan once the tanks are gas-free.
A yacht or passenger vessel in the covered dock: shell plating and tank tops gauged under cover during a refit.
A merchant ship at a repair berth after a port state control deficiency: the affected plating and pipework measured so that repair and re-inspection can be arranged.
A vessel being converted for a new role: baseline gauging of the structure that will carry new loads, supplied to the design team for its calculations.

logistics: Rotterdam The Hague Airport is a short drive from Schiedam, and Amsterdam Schiphol, the main long-haul arrival point, has rail connections to Schiedam Centrum. The yard controls its own gate and induction, so the superintendent or the ship's agent registers the technicians with the yard before they arrive. Team members travelling from India need Schengen visas; for dockings the date is normally known weeks ahead, which gives time to secure visas and fix travel to the yard's planned start.

faqs.q: Can gauging keep pace with a tight Schiedam docking schedule?
faqs.a: That is how we plan it. The team size is set from the TM plan and the number of docking days, and the order of work follows the yard's release of spaces. Readings are shared daily and renewal candidates are marked on the steel, so the yard's planners and the surveyor never wait for the final report to know what has to be cropped.

faqs.q: Does the covered dock make a difference to thickness measurement?
faqs.a: It helps. Bare-steel readings need clean, dry surfaces, and rain or condensation on an open dock floor slows surface preparation and couplant contact. Under a roof, shell gauging can continue through weather that would stop it elsewhere, which matters on a winter docking. The measurement method and the reporting are the same in either dock.

faqs.q: Can you gauge crane pedestals on an offshore vessel at Schiedam?
faqs.a: Yes. Pedestal shells, flanges, foundation plating and the deck structure underneath are gauged, and the welds at the pedestal base and flange are checked for fatigue cracks by magnetic particle testing. This is best done while the crane is off for overhaul or before a new crane is set down, when the surfaces can be prepared and reached without working around a live installation.

faqs.q: What happens if gauging finds more corrosion than the yard specification allowed for?
faqs.a: The readings go to the superintendent as soon as they are taken, with locations, measured thickness and the allowable diminution, so that extra steel can be agreed with the yard while the ship is still in dock. Finding it during the docking beats finding it at the next survey, but finding it before arrival is better still, which is why owners gauge on an earlier call when they can.
